title: Learning Vocabulary in Networks
intro: Meet Ka-yan. The DSE is months away, her vocabulary notebook keeps growing — but the words aren't sticking. Follow one week of her revision and make her choices. You get instant feedback. No account or AI key needed for this part.

scenarios.situation: Ka-yan meets the word 'analyse' in a reading passage. She writes it in her notebook with the Chinese meaning and moves on.
scenarios.question: What would make this word stick better?

options.text: Map its family, partners and near-synonyms
options.feedback: Right. A word is learned when it is connected — family, collocates, near-synonyms. One connected word is worth five isolated ones.

options.text: Write its definition and Chinese translation beside it
options.feedback: That records the word but leaves it isolated — one more entry in a flat list. Meaning sticks when the word is connected: its family (persist, persistence), its partners (persistent effort), its near-synonyms and their differences.

options.text: Add nine more words to round out the list
options.feedback: Ten unrelated words are harder to remember than ten connected ones. Build a network around words from your passage instead.

probe.question: Quick check: what does it mean to know a word as part of a 'network'?

options.text: Knowing its family, partner words and near-synonyms, not just one meaning
options.feedback: Exactly — connections are what make a word retrievable and usable.

options.text: Knowing every dictionary sense of the word by heart
options.feedback: Depth of connections beats breadth of senses — most senses you'll never need.

options.text: Being able to translate it instantly into Chinese
options.feedback: Translation is one link only. Family, collocates and contrasts are what make the word stick.

scenarios.situation: Ka-yan finds 'deteriorate' in a passage about air quality: 'Air quality has deteriorated sharply since 2019.' She is about to ask her tutor what it means.
scenarios.question: What is the best first step?

options.text: Re-read the sentence — what happened, in what pattern?
options.feedback: Yes. The sentence is the anchor — it shows the meaning (got worse), the grammar (intransitive verb), and a partner word (sharply).

options.text: Memorise the definition first, re-read later
options.feedback: Definition-first learning is fragile. Meet the word doing its job in context first; the definition then confirms what you worked out.

options.text: Underline it and come back after finishing the passage
options.feedback: Postponing loses the context you need most. The sentence around the word — what happened, in what pattern — is the raw material for learning it. Capture the sentence now; the passage will still be there.

probe.question: Quick check: what can the surrounding sentence tell you about a new word?

options.text: Its meaning in use, its grammar pattern, and its partner words
options.feedback: Right — one good sentence carries meaning, grammar and collocation all at once.

options.text: Only a rough guess — real meaning comes from the dictionary
options.feedback: The dictionary confirms; the sentence teaches. Context shows the word actually working.

options.text: Its pronunciation and phonetic transcription
options.feedback: Print context can't give you sound — but it gives meaning, grammar and partners, which matter more first.

bullets: Ka-yan wants to ask her tutor
scenarios.transition: The next day — a new passage, a new unknown word.

scenarios.situation: In her practice essay, Ka-yan wrote: 'The government should do more attention to this problem.' Her tutor circled it.
scenarios.question: What kind of error is this, and what is the fix?

options.text: Collocation error — "pay attention", not "do"
options.feedback: Exactly. The meaning was clear but the partnership was wrong. Fluency is mostly knowing which words go together.

options.text: Grammar error — rewrite it in the passive
options.feedback: The grammar is fine. The problem is the word partnership: English says 'pay attention', never 'do attention'.

options.text: Wrong word — replace "attention" entirely
options.feedback: 'Attention' is the right word — it just needs its correct partner verb 'pay'. That's what a collocation is.

probe.question: Quick check: what is a collocation?

options.text: A habitual partnership between words, like 'pay attention' or 'heavy rain'
options.feedback: Yes — collocations are conventional pairings, not logical rules. That's why they must be learned as chunks.

options.text: A grammar rule about the order of subject, verb and object
options.feedback: That's syntax. Collocation is about which words habitually go together, regardless of grammar.

options.text: Two words that share the same meaning
options.feedback: Those are synonyms. Collocations are partners that appear together, like 'make a mistake'.

bullets: The meaning is clear, the wording is off
scenarios.transition: The weekend practice essay comes back with a circle on it.

scenarios.situation: Two of Ka-yan's classmates learned the same 10 words on Monday. Amy re-reads her notes every day. Ben covers his notes, tests himself, then checks.
scenarios.question: Who will remember more by Friday?

options.text: Ben — retrieval beats re-reading, especially spaced
options.feedback: Right. Retrieval practice is one of the most reliable findings in learning science. Struggling to recall IS the learning.

options.text: Amy — daily exposure is the proven method
options.feedback: Re-reading feels safe because the notes look familiar — but familiarity is not recall. Ben's self-testing wins.

options.text: About the same — total time is what counts
options.feedback: Same time, very different results. HOW you practise matters: testing yourself beats reviewing.

probe.question: Quick check: why does self-testing beat re-reading?

options.text: The effort of pulling a word from memory is what strengthens the memory
options.feedback: Exactly — retrieval effort is the workout; re-reading is watching someone else exercise.

options.text: Testing is faster, so you can cover more words per session
options.feedback: Testing is often slower — and that struggle is precisely why it works better.

options.text: Re-reading only works for grammar, not vocabulary
options.feedback: Re-reading is weak for both — the retrieval effect applies to almost everything you learn.

scenarios.transition: Monday. Ka-yan starts watching how her classmates revise.

scenarios.situation: By Friday, Ka-yan can match every one of her 10 words to its meaning in a quiz. Her tutor says she is only halfway there.
scenarios.question: What is the missing half?

options.text: Write sentences combining two or three of them
options.feedback: Yes. Recognising a word (receptive) and using it (productive) are different skills. A word is yours when it appears in YOUR writing.

options.text: Move on — learn 10 more from the next passage
options.feedback: More words without production just makes a longer passive list. Depth first: use this week's words in real sentences.

options.text: Cover the meanings and test yourself recalling each word
options.feedback: Self-testing is excellent — but it is still recognition and recall, the receiving half. The missing half is production: forcing the words into your own sentences, in combination, which is what the exam and real writing demand.

probe.question: Quick check: what is the difference between receptive and productive vocabulary?

options.text: Receptive = understanding a word you meet; productive = using it in your own output
options.feedback: Right — and the receptive-to-productive step is exactly what sentence-writing practises.

options.text: Receptive = spoken words; productive = written words
options.feedback: Both modes can be receptive (listening/reading) or productive (speaking/writing) — the split is understanding vs using.

options.text: Receptive = easy words; productive = advanced words
options.feedback: Difficulty isn't the split — even a simple word is only 'productive' once you can deploy it yourself.

scenarios.transition: Friday. The quiz goes perfectly — almost.

finalCheck.question: You meet a useful new word in a reading passage. What is the FIRST thing to record?

options.text: The sentence it appeared in, plus the pattern around it.
Its dictionary definition, copied in full.
Its definition plus two synonyms from a thesaurus

finalCheck.question: Roughly how many words should one session cover, and why?

options.text: 8–12 connected words — enough to form clusters, few enough for depth.
As many as possible — coverage matters most before the exam.
One word at a time, fully mastered before the next.
"He did a big mistake."
"He maked a mistake."
"He made a mistake."

finalCheck.question: What should the END of every vocabulary session include?

options.text: Writing your own sentences that combine 2–3 of the new words.
Re-reading the full word list three times.
A self-test: cover the list and recall each meaning

agent.name: Word Network Lesson Builder
agent.job: Reads your passage, finds word NETWORKS (groups of related words), asks what you want to improve, and builds a personalised lesson package — slides, quiz, and writing tasks.
agent.knowledge: The network-learning principles from Part A: context first, collocation, retrieval, production — plus this pack's knowledge file.
agent.tools: A language model guided by this pack's SKILL and knowledge files. Publishing uses the platform's Publish button.
workflow: Stage 1 — map 2–3 word networks in your passage and confirm your focus (grammar / word choice / writing)
Stage 2 — deep-dive the chosen network: families, collocates, contrasts, tailored to your focus
Stage 3 — build the lesson package: narrated slides, quiz with feedback, sentence-writing tasks
Stage 4 — coach your own sentences with precise feedback
Stage 5 — teachers: publish it as a live narrated student lesson
agent.guardrails: One stage per reply — never dumps everything at once. Works from real usage patterns only; max 12 target words; never writes your practice sentences for you.
agent.evaluation: Your Stage-4 sentences are the test — the agent checks whether attempt 2 fixes what it flagged, and you rate each deliverable.

intake.label: Paste your reading passage (DSE level, roughly 300–900 words)
What do you most want to improve?
intake.placeholder: grammar / word choice / writing (or a mix)
